d.g: With a crook or bend; with the hand on the hip and elbow turned outward.
d.x: "Now, then, mister," said he, with his head cocked and his arms akimbo, "what are you driving at? Let's have it straight, now."

d.g: With legs spread and the knees bent in an outward or awkward way, sometimes with the feet touching.
Into, in, or of the position where the arms are akimbo.
Of weapons, especially firearms: one held in each hand.
d.x: Although it was a little impractical, Elmer held his revolvers akimbo because to him it looked cool.

akimbo.e: From Middle English in kenebowe, in kene bowe (“in a keen bow”, i.e. “in a sharp bend or angle”), from in (“in”) + keen, kene (“brave, keen, sharp”) + bowe (“bow, bend”). Alternately, possibly from Old Norse kengr (“bent”) + bogi (“a bow”), compare Icelandic kengboginn (“bow-bent”).

d.g: Of persons, of the same kin; related by blood.
d.x: [W]e are too near a kin to lye together, tho' vve may Lodge near one another; […]

d.g: Allied by nature; similar; partaking of the same properties; of the same kind.
d.x: Is not then Fruition near akin to Love?

d.g: To relate or compare; to liken.
d.x: I like to akin the P-Diddy case to Gen-Z's version of the O.J. Simpson trial.

akin.e: From a corruption of of kin, from Middle English of kyn (“related, of kin”), equivalent to a- + kin (1550s). Compare Old English cyn, cynn (“akin, proper, suitable”, adj.).

d.g: apple of Sodom (Calotropis procera).

akvavit.e: Unadapted borrowing from Danish and Swedish akvavit, from Medieval Latin aqua vitae (“water of life”). Doublet of aqua vitae and aquavit. Compare eau-de-vie, whisky, whiskey, and water of life from the same source.
